summary: The appellants were allotted quasi permanent allotment of lands in the village Rai kot . They filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order dated October 31 , 1952 cancelling their allotment on the ground that they had been wrongly fitted in the villages and that there was no evidence to show that these persons were not entitled to allotment of sub urban land as they did not belong to any other class . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of section 19 ( 1 ) of the Act were not applicable to them because it was not shown that they applied to all the allottees who had become evac ue es from Pakistan before the date of cancellation of allotment . In appeal by special leave , HELD : ( i ) Section 19 ( 2 ) is clear that if an allottee has been given a right to be allotted land in the same village or part thereof he shall have preference over others ; but where such right is exercised only after the date mentioned in clause ( d ), then his application would be governed by the provision of section 17 which provides that nothing contained in sections 12 and 19 shall apply to him . [ 10 46 B ] ( ii ) Under section 19 of the , the Custodian General can cancel an allotment if he finds that the allottee ' s claim falls within the scope of section 18 ( 1 ). It is true that the expression " person aggrieved " used in section 19 does not refer to the person against whom action is taken under section 19 . But this provision is general in nature and deals with cases of persons who are not " affected " by the provisions contained in section 9 of the Administration of E vac uee Property Act , 1950 . That being so , the question whether the appellant could be said to be a person aggrieved by the order of the Assistant Custodian rejecting his revision application under section 16 ( 4 ) of that Act could be raised at the time when the order was made . [ 11 C D ]

The respondents were registered dealers under the Bombay Sales Tax Act . They claimed exemption from sales tax on a taxable turnover including purchases of goods sold by them to their buyers in West Bengal , but they continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream and so no tax was real isable on these sales . On the question whether the sale made by the appellant to purchasers who are not registered dealers is liable to be taxed as " sales of goods ", HELD : ( 1 ) The words " a person " in section 10 ( b ) mean a registered dealer and not an unregistered dealer . [ 11 B ] ( 2 ) The word " a " used in section 8 ( b ), must be given its natural meaning without any doubt or ambiguity . It does not mean that all sales effected by a registered assessee should be subjected to tax irrespective of the fact whether such sales have taken place within the State of Bombay or outside it . If the intention of the Legislature was to levy purchase tax only if the goods were actually despatched outside the State , then there would be no need for making a declaration of intention to sell the goods at all . [ 12 G H ; 13 A C ] ( 3 ) In order to make the declaration of the intention clear , it has to be shown that the goods which were actually delivered were intended to be purchased by the purchasing dealer himself . There is nothing in the language of the section which requires that the declaration should be made before the delivery of the certificate . The purpose of the declaration contemplated by the section is to enable the purchaser to obtain the benefit of the exemption provided by the notification . When he sells the goods to another person , he becomes the owner thereof . He may not be aware of the actual transaction of the sale . But when he sells his goods to others , he is not a registered purchaser because the goods are not available to him . Therefore , the use of the words " one who is not registered dealer " in clause ( b ). of the Explanation to section 10 cannot be said to be a deliberate act with the intention to evade payment of tax . [ 14 D E ]

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 , I . P . C ., and sentenced to death for committing the murder of Sheo Sahai and sentenced him to imprisonment for life . He appealed to the High Court against his conviction and sentence but failed . The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentences passed on him . In appeal to this Court it was contended that ( 1 ) there was no evidence in support of the prosecution case which could justify an inference that the appellant had committed the murder ; ( 2 ) the circumstances relied upon by the trial court were not such as would lead to the only conclusion that the accused alone knew what he did with the deceased and therefore the presumption arising under section 106 of the Evidence Act could not be made use of . HELD : ( i ) There is nothing in the statement of the appellant recorded by the police officer where he said that he had seen the dead body of Sheo Swarup at night or that he saw the dead man lying near a tree while going towards the Police Station . [ 10 31 E ] ( ii ) The fact that the dead person was found lying near the well of one Mah mood after the incident clearly shows that the story about the murder must have been made out . It cannot be said that the circumstance relied upon was so improbable as to give rise to a reasonable doubt regarding the guilt of the accused . [ 11 31 B D ] ( iii ) The conduct of the deceased immediately after the occurrence showed that she was not in a position to tell the truth when she went to the Police station and reported the matter to her brother who was present at the Police Post . She also stated that she had told the appellant ' s brother that he should go to the village and report the matter . But the explanation given by the appellant was that she did not know how to proceed to the police station and report dictated by the deceased . [ 32 G H ] ( iv ) The evidence led by the prosecution was sufficient to prove that the deceased was murdered before she left the house and that the evidence adduced by the defence was sufficient enough to establish that the murder took place inside the house of the wife of the witness . [ 33 A B ]

The appellant was a partnership firm carrying on business as a limited company with effect from November 13 , 1947 . On February 7 , 1948 , the two brothers entered into an agreement for sale of their share holdings in the appellant ' s family and agreed to sell their shares to the appellant at certain rates . In pursuance of that agreement they paid Rs . 1 , 000 by way of advance but did not pay any further amount . They were however , asked to make good the balance of the consideration within 15 days failing which the appellant would be entitled to get interest @ 12 % per annum on the sum due till the date of payment . The appellant claimed relief under section 25 ( 4 ) of the Income tax Act , 1922 , read with section 26 ( 2 ) of that Act . The Tribunal held that there had been a succession between the three brothers and therefore it could not be said that there was a succession within the meaning of section 26 . Held : ( i ) It is well settled that if one who owns property or assets , dies leaving behind his widow and children , then only the other person who has acquired a right to succeed to the estate of the deceased can claim relief under Section 25 ( 2 ). But where the deceased died without having any issue , he being the sole heir of the last owner , the question whether the death took place during the life time of the exec utor or after his death does not arise . ( ii ) Where a person dies leaving no legal heir except the real surviving member of the joint family , the court will have regard to the fact whether the deceased left him surviving as a result of the death of the person succeeding to the property of the adop tive father . If the deceased leaves no heir capable of taking care of the properties of the natural father , such as a manager , trustee etc ., the Court may hold that the adopted son was alive when the suit was filed .

The respondent was a resident of the former State of Rajasthan . He applied for and obtained a permit for export of 15 , 000 ma unds of ch uni from the former Dholpur State on June 28 , 1947 and remained in force upto December 2 , 1947 . On July 1 , 1947 the United State of Jaipur passed the Rajasthan Excise Duties Ordinance 1949 which provided that no liquor shall be exported from the latter State until the expiry of six months after the date of its issue or before the commencement of the Rajasthan excise Duties Ordinance , 1949 . The appellant filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution claiming refund of the excess amount paid to him as duty on the ground that he had not been granted any licence for export ation of the goods . The High Court held that the agreement did not confer any right on the appellant to claim refund of excess amount but only the right to claim rebate and that the contract was void because it was made by the Rul er of Jodhpur and therefore the agreement could not be said to have been recognised by the new sovereign . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The agreement was not a law within the meaning of article 286 of the Co ven ant . [ 184 D ] ( ii ) The terms of the agreement were not intended to be implied unless there was anything repugnant in the subject or context . It is clear from the language of the document that the terms of a statute are not necessarily implied . There can be no question of recognition by the Union of India . [ 185 G H ; 186 A B ] ( iii ) The expression " in accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act " has to be read in the light of the context in which they appear . If the intention of the legislature was to exclude the exemption from income tax and excise duty , then the exemption would be available if the conditions laid down therein were satisfied . [ 187 C E ]

The appellant contended that in the absence of an agreement between the Government and the then Jagir dar dar dar the appellant had been paid tax on the basis of 1 / 4th of the revenue . The High Court held : " The question referred to it in this appeal must be decided by the courts below as the Tribunal may decide the nature of the transaction . The respondents challenged the validity of the orders passed by the Appellate Authority . The appeals were dismissed by the High Court . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The issue before the High court was whether the appellant ' s contention was that the amount payable was due from the appellant to the Government but could not be said to have been included in the assessment years 1949 50 per cent . The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1956 . It had a factory at A lex andra , and it carried on its business from that place to its head office situated at Bombay . In 1959 , the Company entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the sale of certain machinery including the machinery installed by the Company . Under this agreement the Company agreed to sell all its assets and liabilities to the purchasers subject to the terms and conditions set out therein . Clause ( 2 ) of the agreement provided that the purchaser shall not be entitled to any compensation or damages against the Company if the Company failed to carry out the terms of the contract within 30 days after the expiry of the period mentioned in clause ( 1 ). The Company did not pay any compensation as required under cl s . ( 3 ), ( 4 ) and ( 5 ) of Art . III of the Agreement . On December 15 , 1953 , the Union served a notice upon the Company calling upon it to show cause why the amount should not be recovered from it . The Company replied contending that the Company was liable to pay the amount due to it . By a letter dated January 19 , 1955 , the President of the Company informed the Company that the amount would be paid only after the termination of the agency and that the payment would be made after the expiration of the term of the Agency . The company also stated that the amounts were payable only after termination of agency and therefore there was no question of any claim being barred by limitation . The Tribunal held that the Union was not entitled to recover the amount because the Union had not been able to establish that the workmen were entitled to receive the amount . The High Court dismissed the petition . Held : ( i ) The liability to pay compensation arises when the services are terminated before the expiry or termination of service ; but where the services have been terminated without giving one month ' s notice or wages in lieu thereof , the liability is attracted by the fact that the employment has continued till the termination thereof . ( ii ) The scheme of the agreements clearly shows that the obligation to pay bonus is on the employer and not on the workmen . If the employees do not work during the period they are entitled to the same rate of wages as those employed in the corresponding post ure , then the liability will arise even after the completion of the job . The appellant bank was a banking company . It had been carrying on business in the nature of banking , and its working hours were from January 1 , 1959 to April 30 , 1960 . On March 31 , 1961 the Bank issued a notice under section 33 C ( 2 ) of the Industrial Disputes Act , 1947 , for determining the pay scales of workmen employed in banks which were not governed by the Sas try Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal decision dated August 26 , 1963 . In the first group of appeals before this Court it was contended that the award did not state any reasons for fixing the pay scale at Rs . 175 but only stated that the employees would be fitted in the new scales of pay provided by the Desai award . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : ( i ) The award is clear and specific . There is no reason why the clerical staff should have been given the higher pay than what they are entitled to under sub cl . ( d ) of cl . 29 of the Sas ty Award . [ 1009 B ] ( ii ) The tribunal has made an error in holding that the revised pay scale of Rs . 182 with effect from January l , 1962 was fixed at Rs , 170 . The High Court erred in taking the view that the original pay scale was Rs . 184 and not Rs . 112 . [ 1010 E G ] ( iii ) The High Courts order is correct and does not suffer from any infirmity . [ 1011 D ] ( iv ) The scheme of dearness allowance is based upon the basic pay in the Sas ri ' s case and there is nothing wrong or illegal in fixing the same at Rs 108 . The minimum pay in that cadre is Rs . 180 . That being so , the maximum pay prescribed by the award cannot be fixed at more than Rs . 108 . [ 1012 A ]

The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Caste . He challenged the validity of the election on various grounds , namely ( 1 ) that he belonged to a Scheduled Caste ; and ( 2 ) that his nomination paper had been improperly rejected by the Returning Officer . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant did not belong to any caste which was included in the list of Scheduled Castes . On appeal , the High Court held that the declaration of the appellant as belonging to a scheduled caste was invalid because it was made after due enquiry and therefore void . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) There is no doubt that the question whether a person belongs to a reserved category or not has to be decided in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution . [ 389 E ] ( ii ) The test for determining whether a particular caste is a Scheduled Tribe or not is whether the caste is included in a list of backward classes . If the caste of a person is included within the list , then the caste would have been included in such list . But if the castes are included in an earlier list , they cannot be considered as belonging either to a tribe or to some other class . [ 390 A B ]

The appellant was appointed as a jail or in the alternative to his parent State . Held , that the appellant was entitled to a decree for Rs . 2 , 690 , 919 being arrears of his pay and allowances during the period when he was working at Sur Kheda District Jail . The appellant ' s claim for arrears of salaries and the State of Maharashtra ' s petition challenging the validity of the proceedings before the High Courts was barred by limitation . The High Court was wrong in holding in favour of the respondent .

The assessee , a firm carrying on business at Bombay as importers of yarn and also as agents for the sale proceeds of cotton yarn sold by it to its customers in Bombay , filed returns showing profits from sales made to various parties . In the assessment year 1952 53 , the Income tax Officer disallowed the deduction claimed under section 10 ( 2 ) ( vi ) of the Indian Income Tax Act , 1922 on the ground that the amounts were not received by the assessee in his own name but in the name of his wife and daughter . On appeal , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sums were not liable to be deducted as those were paid out of the income of the assessee ' s business . He further found that the amount was not credited into the accounts of the appellant company or any other person except the assessee who had been given credit for payment of interest on loans taken by him . The Tribunal however allowed the claim holding that the sum of Rs . 2 , 68 , 385 / was not an allowable expenditure because no part of the amount could have been debited to the profit and loss account of the respondent firm . The High Court answered the question against the Department . Dismis sing the appeal to this Court , HELD : 1 . It is well settled that if there is some reasonable basis for the conclusion that the money was not sent to the assessee for which he has incurred the liability , then the same must be shown to have been received by him in the ordinary course of his business . [ 423 C D ] 2 . The fact that the moneys were sent to a different concern does not mean that they are received in the usual course of the business of the asses ee . They are received by one concern only when the entire amount is transferred to another concern . If the money is not so transferred to the other concern , it cannot be said that the monies were not sent by the appellant to the Bombay firm in the normal course of its business . There is nothing in the statement of case to show that the funds sent to Bombay firm were not actually received by it in the course of their business . Therefore , the finding with regard to the whole of the consideration received by way of loan from the Bombay Company is correct . [ 424 F G ; 425 A B ] 3 . The petitioner company was a private limited company and its shares were acquired by the Government of India . In order to acquire , in the public interest , the shares of certain foreign companies which had been purchased from outside abroad for the purpose of carrying on business as share brokers and other persons it appointed an auditor under section 2 ( 1 ) of the Indian Income tax Act to conduct an investigation into the affairs of the said company . On the 12th April 1954 , the Central Government referred the question whether the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act , 1947 , should be applied to the case of the petitioner company . The Commission after hearing the parties passed an order dated the 11th March 1955 , directing that the proceedings against the petitioner should not proceed without obtaining the previous permission of the Reserve Bank of India before proceeding with the inquiry . The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid provision but the High Court dismissed the same holding that there was no violation of article 14 of the Constitution . It also held that the provisions contained in section 5 ( 4 ) of Act XXX of 1947 could not be invoked because the provisions Of section 34 of the Act did not apply to the present case . Held : ( i ) Section 5 ( 1 )( c ) of Ordinance No . XX VII of 1949 is valid and intra vires inasmuch as it provides that all proceedings pending immediately before the commencement of the ordin ance shall continue to be dealt with under the corresponding provisions of the repealed Ordinance unless they are covered by the saving clause provided therein or any other similar provision of the Ordinance . ( ii ) The procedure prescribed by the impugned Act does not suffer from the vice of discrimination or ine quality between two procedures . Under the provisions , of the impugned enactment ి the procedure prescribed in sections 6 & 7 of Act XL II of 1949 has been followed ; ( iii ) the procedure laid down in sections 37 and 38 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies only to cases where the offences have been committed within the territory of India and the person proceeded against is charged with such offence in relation to the commission of those offences .

The appellants were convicted for the same offence and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for 5 years . They filed a petition under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code , and sentences of 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs . 100 / each . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption in regard to the guilt of the accused was not attracted as the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption . It was further urged that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was unreliable because they had been believed by the trial court and the High Court and there was no reason why the conviction should be set aside . Held : ( i ) The presumption is strong er when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is . There is no doubt that the accused persons were guilty of the offence of dacoity . But if the accused are proved to have committed the murder of some other person or persons who were prosecuted as offenders and who were tried as offenders then the presumption would arise that the offender was concerned with the commission of the crime itself . If the accused were guilty then the burden of proof would shift to the accused . The presumption does not depend upon the facts of each case but only on the circumstances of each particular case . The appellant , a partnership firm , was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61 . In its return filed under section 139 of the Income Tax Act 1961 , it claimed that in respect of certain assessment years , there were no " good and sufficient reasons " for the assessee ' s failure to file his return within time as required by section 151 ( 2 ) of the Act . The Income tax Officer rejected this claim on the ground that he had not given any reason why the returns should be accepted . On appeal , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice issued under section 148 was invalid because : ( i ) the assessee did not submit the return within the prescribed period ; ( ii ) the return submitted by him was incomplete and therefore could not be entertained ; and ( iii ) the assessment proceedings were barred by limitation . The High Court dismissed the petition . Dismis sing the appeal to this Court , HELD : ( 1 ) There is nothing in section 147 or section 149 which requires that where an assessee has failed to furnish a return within one year from the end of the relevant assessment year , the assessing authority may serve upon him a notice under section 149 requiring him to show cause why he should not be assessed to tax . [ 10 31 B ] ( 2 )( a ) Section 147 does not require that every notice must specify the grounds on which the assessment can be made . It is only when the requirements of clause ( b ) are satisfied that the Income tax officer has to issue a notice . If the requirement of clause 2 ( d ) is complied with , the order passed by the Income - tax Officer would be without jurisdiction . [ 1032 E F ] ( b ). The words " reasonable opportunity " used in section 151 have been construed by courts to mean " reasonable opportunities ". They do not mean " all necessary " or " reasonably practicable " but they are con jun ctive ly used in the context in which they occur . The word " reasonable " means " fair and just " and not " impossible ". [ 1033 C D ] ( c ) The expression " reasonable requirement " in section 148 includes not merely the existence of some condition precedent to the issue of a notice but also the sufficiency of the material before the Income TAX Officer on the basis of which he forms the requisite opinion . The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Cor ps Training Centre , Sec und r abad . He was attached with the Army , Ordnance Cor p . Workshop , Sec u und r hat , and was posted as such at the Unit lines of 51 1 1 Gur kha Rifles where he arranged his meeting with a se po y . On April 4 , 1958 , he committed acts of misconduct by removing him from service . In March 1959 , he was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct . The Central Government found it to be unsatisfactory and on April 9 , 1959 , an order was passed terminating the services of the respondent . The High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to any relief under article 311 ( 2 ) of the Constitution . Held : ( i ) The words " subject to the provisions of this Act " occurring in section 19 are wide enough to include all kinds of punishments for misconduct or other similar offences . The word " subject " is defined in section 2 ( e ) of that Act which means " any person subject to this Act ". Section 3 provides that no person subject shall be deemed to have been appointed to hold office during the pleasure of the President until the expiration of one year after the expiry of the term of office of the Governor of India or the Governor General in Council or the Chief Minister or the Lieutenant Governor of the Union Territory concerned ; ( ii ) " subject of course to the provision of this act " means " to give power to the President to remove a person from the service of persons subject to that Act ."

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department , Pep su . He was charged with an offence under section 465 of the Indian Penal Code for having received Rs . 51 from the accused as illegal gratification and that he had not done any official duty or acted in excess of his authority . The prosecution case was that on the date when the appellant was put up by the police at the Police Station he had received Rs , 51 from one Ram Singh who was a clerk in the office of the District Magistrate , Patiala , which amount was paid to him by the latter . On the basis of this payment , the appellant ' s explanation was found to be false and therefore prosecuted . Held , that sanction was necessary before cognizance could be taken against the appellant . It is well settled that where a public servant acts malic iously and fraudulently , it is not sufficient that he should have obtained the sanction of the Government . In the present case , the act complained of did not fall within the scope of his duties , but merely because the money was paid into the treasury , and the question whether the act was done in execution of the duty or not would depend upon the facts of each case .

The appellant , a company registered under the Indian Companies Act 1913 , was a " commercial establishment " within the meaning of section 2 ( 5 ) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act , 1954 . The primary objects of the Federation as set out in its Memorandum of Association were " to promote the business of the firm ". The object of the Union was to provide for an industrial establishment for the benefit of the members of the public and to secure the interests of the general public . In order that the said object should be so provided , it was felt necessary to make arrangements for the spread of commercial and social activities and to provide facilities for the working of the industry . It was also decided by the Government that the provisions of the Act would not apply to the undertaking of the association which had been established for the purpose of carrying on the business or trade of the Association . The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned judgment . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was a commercial establishment within the definition of Section 2 ( 1 )( f ) of Delhi Shops & Establishments Act . The appeal was allowed . On appeal by certificate the High court held that the expression ' trade or business ' in section 11 of the said Act did not include any activity carried on by the appellant but only incidental to the main object of making the Act applicable to the establishment of the respondent . The State appealed to this Court . Held : ( i ) The word " trade " in section 2 is wide enough to include all activities carried on in the course of trade or profession ; ( ii ) The words " trade or Business " do not necessarily mean anything by which one person may be able to carry on his trade or occupation , but merely means something by which another person may not be able either to carry out the trade or use it for some other purpose . The word ' trade ' does not necessarily imply something by whatever name called . The dictionary meaning of the word ' commerce ' is " trade , business or profession " and the word " manufacture " in the context means bringing about any change in the substance of the commodity or goods . The expression " trade ", therefore , cannot be construed in a narrow sense . The question whether the activity of the appellant amounts to " trade ". must depend upon the intention of the legislature . If the words " dealing with " are used in the same sense , they will have to be read as " trade ." The word ` trade ' has not been defined in the Act .

The appellants were manufacturers of " Cinema Ar c Carbon s " manufactured by them . They claimed that they had been purchased by persons other than those who ran cin em as or for any other use . The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the goods under consideration were covered by entry No . 4 of the 1st Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act , 1957 and that the sales tax authorities were bound to consider the use which is ordinarily made of the ar c carbon s . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the entry in question links the taxable object with its general or ordinary use . It was further urged that the words " parts thereof " are used in various entries , such as entry No ., 6 of the First Schedule to Andhra Pradesh ( General Sales tax ) Act , 1958 , and the word ' accessories ' in the said entry must be construed accordingly . The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 1952 1952 by the Third Income tax Officer , C 1 Ward , Bombay . In respect of his own business he was assessed as a result of which he had been sentenced to pay a fine of Rs . 40 , 178 4 . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Superintendent of Estate , but in appeal the Collector held that the assessee was not liable to be prosecuted under section 13 ( 2 ) of the Act because it was not proved that the income from the business was exempt from liability to tax . On appeal the Appellate Tribunal upheld the view taken by the authorities below . It also held that there was no evidence on record to show that the appellant was guilty of concealment or suppression of facts . Held , that the expression " concealment " used in section 13 of the Indian Income Tax Act is wide enough to include any omission or commission on the part of the assessee . The word " concealment ' has not been defined in the Act . The words " concealment ", " wilful default " and " willful default " are sy non y mous with " intentional default ". The term " concealment of facts " means intention to evade payment of tax . The fact that the person who made the statement was not examined before the assessing officer and the appellate authority did not examine him would not make the statement of the person making the statement inadmissible . The mere fact that he made the statements were not sufficient to cover the certified demand , does not mean that the burden of proof was on the assessee to prove that the statement had been made voluntarily . The failure to produce the books of account and other documents before the Assessing Officer could not lead to the conclusion that the maker of the statement knew what might have happened to the assessee and that the onus was discharged .

The petitioners who were working as Sub Inspectors of Police in the Andhra Pradesh State , filed writ petitions challenging the validity of certain amendments made to the Fundamental Rules by which they were given retrospective effect from January 1 , 1972 . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The power conferred by the Proviso to Article 309 is of a legislative character and is to be exercised by the Legislature ; its power to amend any part of the Fundamental rules cannot be taken away except by express provision or by necessary intendment . [ 591 C ] ( ii ) The amending power under the proviso is subject to the limitations placed by article 309 . It has been held by this Court that the power to legislate is not an absolute one but is hed ged with limitations . The power to make laws is derived from the Constitution itself and if the legislature by appropriate means makes a law , it can enact a law which comes into force only when it fram es the law and the procedure for doing so must have some effect . If the exercise of the power is outside the permissible limits , it would amount to encroachment upon the judicial power . Therefore , the amendment made to Rule 2 ( a ) by G . O . Ms . The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death . His appeal to the High Court failed , but his conviction s were maintained on the ground that there was no evidence to show that he had committed the murder of one person or more than one persons in furtherance of their common intention . Held : ( 1 ) That a sentence of imprisonment for life is an extreme penalty so far as it relates to the crime of murder is concerned ; if two Judges concur in the commission of the offence by the same act , then only this Court can interfere with the discretion of the Judge who has imposed the sentence . In the present case , however , the High Courts have not accepted the verdict of the trial court because they differ ed from the opinion of the two judges regarding the guilt of the accused . There are cases where the High court should be slow to interfere with its judgment and substitute its own discretion for that of the Sessions Judge . But when the High courts come to conclusion that the order of acquittal passed by them was wrong , there is nothing in law which prevents them from doing so . It is well settled that the power of review available to the Supreme Court under article 137 of the Constitution is wide and the very fact that the High C ount has made certain observations against the appellate Judges does not mean that such powers must be exercised sparingly .

They contended that in view of the provisions contained in Rule 2 ( x )( 2 ) read with Rule 12 of the Rules , they were entitled to sell their entire stock for sale at the price fixed by the State Government under the said rule ; that the impugned notification was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it did not fix any minimum quantity of liquor which could be sold by retail and thus violated Articles 14 , 19 ( 1 ) ( g ), 304 ( b ) and 301 of the constitution ; and that the action taken by the respondents amounted to an infringement of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19 ( i )( g ) of th e Constitution . On behalf of the respondent State it was submitted that the power conferred on the State Legislature under section 2 ( d ) of ' the Act is wide enough to include all kinds of intoxic ants including liquid chemicals and intoxicating drugs and therefore the State has no power to regulate the possession or sale of such articles . The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Travancore and it had its registered office in British India . It filed its return for the assessment year 1948 49 , showing an income of Rs . 11 , 872 for the previous years ending June 30 , 1949 , and December 31 , 1949 . In respect of the first two appeals the Appellate Tribunal held that the business loss incurred by the assessee during those years was not liable to be included in the total income of the assessee under section 10 ( 1 ) of the Indian Income tax Act 1922 . On appeal by special leave the appellant contended that the High Court erred in holding that the proviso to section 24 ( 1 )( b ) of Travancore Act did not apply to the case of the second proviso to sub clause ( i ) of section 24 of the Travancore Act as it applied only to cases where the profits or gains were taxable in the hands of the asses se if they arose outside the State . Held : ( 1 ). The proviso to subsection ( 1 ), which is a general provision dealing with computation of agricultural income , applies to all cases falling within the category mentioned therein ; but the proviso does not say that such cases must be deemed to have arisen in any part of the State from which the income has been derived . ( 2 ) The proviso is intended to deal with cases of persons who are resident in the taxable territories and whose income is being computed under the head ' Prof its and gains of business in British Indian States '. Therefore , the words " business in the Indian State " occurring in the proviso do not refer to business in another State . ( 3 ) Section 32 ( 1 ): does not expressly mention the word " business " in the main part of section 10 . But this would make no difference because the proviso refers to business which is carried on in the territory of India . ( 4 ) The Explanation to section 10 of the Act does not refer only to business of the kind referred to in section 10 , namely , the business of banking , and therefore it cannot be said that the legislature intended to exclude business in a foreign country from the operation of the proviso . ( 5 ) The object of the Explanation is to explain the meaning of the expression " business ". If the Legislature wanted to include business in one place in the other then the explanation would have used the words ' business in India ' also . The appellants were the first offenders . They filed a complaint against the respondent No . 1 under section 31 ( 1 ) read with section 33 of the , and also under section 33 ( 1 )( b ) of the Act alleging that they had committed offences punishable under sections 31 ( i ), 32 ( 2 ) and 33 ( 3 ) of t he , and section 33 A of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as the conciliation proceedings could not be said to have concluded in the case where no settlement is arrived at , the appellants should be held guilty under section 12 ( 6 ) of that Act . HELD : ( i ) Section 12 ( 5 ) of 1947 provides for the submission of report by the Conciliation Officer within 14 days from the date of receipt of the report by him . It is true that section 12 of 1947 empowers the State Government to make an order directing the inquiry into any matter referred to in section 10 or section 11 of the 1946 Act . But section 12 does not contemplate that the report must be made and the proceedings closed after 15 days . [ 739 D ] ( ii ) The provisions of sub section 2 ( b ) are mandatory and do not support the contention of the appellant that the inquiry should be deemed to have commenced when the report is received by the appropriate Government . The termination of the conciliation proceeding can only be done if there is a settlement between the parties or if the conciliation officer does not make his report within 14 months . [ 741 E F ]
